title: CS6460 Module 1 · Scene quiz
note: Audit bank: lecture scenes → paraphrase choices (not vocab titles). Built from Module 1 clean extracts, not Canvas stems.

items.stem: A student can recite that mass does not change free-fall acceleration. In lab they still bet the heavier ball hits first, and look surprised when both land together. Which claim fits Joyner's constructivist account?

choices.text: The gut prediction comes from a personal mental model that was never rebuilt, even though the sentence was stored.
Learning failed because the teacher never rewarded the correct verbal answer often enough.
The student learned by building a shareable demo; the public artifact is what counts as knowledge.
Reciting the fact means the file transferred; the surprise is only test anxiety.

items.explain: Constructivism (Piaget framing in Joyner): knowledge is a rebuilt mental model, not a download. Recitation without model change is the classic tell. Not behaviorism (rewards only), not constructionism (external artifact).

items.stem: Both balls land together. The student shrugs that the apparatus must be rigged, keeps predicting heavy-wins next round, and never revises the fall rule. What is happening to the mental model?

choices.text: New experience is bent to fit the old model; the schema itself stays put.
The model is rewritten so predictions will flip next time.
The mismatch is being left unresolved on purpose as the whole goal of the lesson.
A peer tutor is temporarily doing the hard part so the student can succeed.

items.explain: Assimilation: force the odd result into the old box (trick / fluke). Accommodation would rewrite the rule. Disequilibrium is the mismatch feeling; scaffolding/MKO is support from outside.

items.stem: After several undeniable equal landings, the student stops calling the demo a trick and starts predicting both balls together. Which move describes the change?

choices.text: The mental structures themselves were reshaped to fit the new experience.
The conflict was explained away so the old prediction could survive.
Only outward behavior changed; no claim is made about an inner model.
The student built a public physics toy; that outside make is the learning theory in play.

items.explain: Accommodation = reshape the model. Assimilation protects the old model. Behaviorism stays on observables. Constructionism centers the external artifact.

items.stem: In Logo, a learner drives a turtle with forward/turn commands. The drawing comes out lopsided. Joyner treats that wrong drawing as useful. Why?

choices.text: The mismatch between intended path and what appeared forces the learner to rethink the rule.
Wrong drawings should be hidden so motivation stays high.
The turtle is mainly a reward dispenser for correct syntax.
Logo exists to deliver geometry facts by lecture with a cute cursor.

items.explain: Logo turtle + immediate feedback → productive disequilibrium (and constructionism's debugging habit). Error is information, not shame.

items.stem: Joyner spends time on Logo. What is it, in course voice?

choices.text: A language plus a turtle you drive with forward/turn — floor robot first, then on-screen — so geometry and coding happen together.
MIT's 2007 block language with low floor, high ceiling, and wide walls.
A 1998 robotics kit named after Papert's book.
Physical bricks wired so Logo code controls motors and lights.

items.explain: Logo = Papert's turtle language. Scratch = 2007 blocks. LEGO Mindstorms = 1998 kit. LEGO/Logo = late-1980s bricks+code (Resnick & Ocko).

items.stem: Late 1980s at MIT: Mitchel Resnick and Stephen Ocko connect physical LEGO to code. What is that lineage object?

choices.text: LEGO/Logo — programs show up as motion, light, or sound in the bricks.
Scratch — drag blocks to make unrelated kids' projects on one tool.
Capital-D Direct Instruction — scripted choral responses with field-tested lessons.
PLATO/TUTOR — an early intelligent tutoring system lineage.

items.explain: LEGO/Logo is the bricks+Logo bridge. Scratch comes later (2007). DI and ITS are different lessons.

items.stem: A quiz stem mentions LEGO Mindstorms (1998). How does Joyner relate it to Papert?

choices.text: The kit is named after Papert's 1980 book Mindstorms; book = theory, kit = later toy.
Papert invented the 1998 kit before writing any book.
Mindstorms is Resnick's name for the Four P's.
Mindstorms is Engelmann's scripted reading program.

items.explain: Book 1980, kit 1998 named after the book. Four P's are Resnick. Engelmann is Direct Instruction.

items.stem: One student rebuilds an inner prediction after a sim. Another learns mainly by shipping a game classmates can click. Joyner's TIV vs TION split?

choices.text: First is constructivism (mental model); second is constructionism (external make drives learning).
First is constructionism; second is constructivism.
Both are behaviorism because something observable changed.
Both are instructionism because a teacher designed the activity.

items.explain: Constructivism = inside rebuild. Constructionism = public artifact as the engine. They stack; they are not typos.

items.stem: Same tool: one kid makes a story, another makes a game, both personally meaningful. Resnick's add beyond low floor / high ceiling is?

choices.text: Wide walls — many kinds of projects people care about, not only many ages or devices.
Faultless communication — confusion is always the student's fault.
Variable-ratio reinforcement — likes and slots for persistence.
Image Principle — show the instructor's face beside the slides.

items.explain: Wide walls (Resnick). Floor/ceiling from Papert line. Other options are other lessons and wrong.

items.stem: A child figures out a Logo path by walking the room as the turtle, then writing commands that match what they walked. Papert's name for that?

choices.text: Understand the program by acting it out with your own body.
Improve learning mainly by perfecting how teachers lecture.
Fit odd results into the old schema so nothing inside changes.
Remove dessert to decrease unfinished-dinner behavior.

items.explain: Body-syntonic (Papert). Instructionism is better telling. Assimilation is schema-protect. Negative punishment is dessert.

items.stem: A makerspace tells novices to 'just explore' with no worked examples. Many drown or invent wrong rules. Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark (2006) would say?

choices.text: Learning being constructive does not mean beginners should get minimal guidance; novices need strong guidance first.
Constructivism as a theory of mental models is false.
Novices always learn best with zero instruction.
Only Capital-D Direct Instruction scripts are allowed forever.

items.explain: KSC attacks unguided teaching, not 'learners build models.' Guidance advantage recedes with high prior knowledge.

items.stem: Teacher solves one problem aloud, then solves with the class, then students solve alone. Pearson and Gallagher's arc?

choices.text: I do, we do, you do — responsibility moves to the learner.
You discover first, then the teacher consolidates only if needed.
Pay students for puzzles so free-time play increases.
Match teaching style to visual vs auditory preference.

items.explain: Gradual release. Productive failure flips the order (struggle then teach hard). Deci payment cut free play. Learning styles = myth.

items.stem: A scripted program treats student confusion as a flaw in the materials: if the student hasn't learned, the teacher hasn't taught. Which lineage?

choices.text: Engelmann / Becker Direct Instruction — faultless communication.
Papert instructionism — perfect the lecture and get out of the way of making.
Rogoff guided participation — learn only by cooking beside an adult.
Reich Matthew effect — tools help the already-ahead first.

items.explain: Capital-D DI credo. Papert's instructionism is the 'better transmission' foil to constructionism — different claim.

items.stem: Joyner contrasts a Minecraft sandbox with a LEGO booklet that shows steps. Which is closer to direct instruction?

choices.text: The LEGO booklet — explicit modeled steps toward a build.
The Minecraft sandbox — open explore with no modeled path.
Neither; both are classical conditioning.
Only remote proctoring counts as direct instruction.

items.explain: Lecture line: Minecraft sandbox is not di; LEGO booklet is. Sandbox can be constructionist explore.

items.stem: A parent turns off a disliked phone time-limit only after chores are done. Chore-doing goes up. What happened?

choices.text: Something disliked was removed, and the behavior increased — reinforcement, not punishment.
Something disliked was added, so the behavior should decrease.
Something liked was removed to decrease a behavior.
An automatic fear response transferred from a bell to a test.

items.explain: Negative reinforcement: remove dislike → behavior up. Positive punishment adds dislike. Negative punishment removes like. Classical is Pavlov pairing.

items.stem: Dinner unfinished → dessert taken away → unfinished dinners become less common. Classify the consequence.

choices.text: Remove something liked so the unwanted behavior goes down.
Remove something disliked so a desired behavior goes up.
Add praise so the desired behavior goes up.
Pair a neutral cue with stress until the cue alone stresses.

items.explain: Negative punishment. Negative reinforcement would remove dislike to increase a behavior. Ask up/down first, then add/remove.

items.stem: Bell with food until bell alone makes drool; later, tests pair with stress the same way. Which learning?

choices.text: Classical conditioning — an automatic response transfers across paired stimuli.
Operant shaping — reinforce closer approximations of a voluntary act.
Metacognitive monitoring — judge whether you understand the chapter.
Legitimate peripheral participation — low-stakes real work at the edge of a group.

items.explain: Pavlov / classical (involuntary). Operant is voluntary consequences. Other options are other modules.

items.stem: Why does Joyner say cognitivism had to open the black box that behaviorism left closed?

choices.text: Observable S–R alone could not explain abstract ideas, transfer, or truly novel solving.
Rewards never change behavior, so the whole field collapsed.
Pavlov proved mental models are photographs of experience.
Only AI connectionism counts as psychology now.

items.explain: Behaviorism incomplete for mind-like phenomena; cognitivism keeps rigor but studies internal processing.

items.stem: A tutor only says 'wrong, try again.' Another says why the step failed and what rule to revise. Cognitivist preference?

choices.text: Explain why — update the mental model, not only nudge the next click.
Never explain; only variable-ratio points.
Always show the instructor's face while narrating.
Match the hint style to the learner's visual style.

items.explain: Cognitivist feedback fixes understanding. Image Principle says the face usually does not help. Learning styles myth.

items.stem: A narrated lesson adds cute unrelated animations and a talking head that repeats the same words. Mayer-line claims Joyner primed?

choices.text: Non-teaching visuals can hurt (coherence); the face usually adds no new info and can steal attention (image).
More visuals always help because dual channel has no limit.
Only the face hurts; decorative clip-art always helps motivation enough to offset load.
Extraneous load is good because desirable difficulties include clutter.

items.explain: Coherence = cut non-semantic visuals. Image = face on narrated lesson usually doesn't help. Desirable difficulties are content struggle, not junk UI.

items.stem: Notes feel smooth after rereading. Practice quiz is blank. What went wrong?

choices.text: Familiarity was mistaken for ability to recall — fluency illusion.
Negative reinforcement removed the quiz stress.
Wide walls prevented a single correct project.
Classical conditioning paired the notes with food.

items.explain: Fluency illusion / calibration failure. Practice quizzes recalibrate judgments of learning.

items.stem: A student clicks every hint immediately to finish points without struggling. Joyner's metacognition / help-seeking framing?

choices.text: Executive / over-reliant help-seeking — or gaming the system — instead of adaptive help after real try.
Ideal scaffolding because support should never fade.
Mastery goals, because looking smart to peers is the aim.
Body-syntonic reasoning via the hint button.

items.explain: Adaptive help-seeking vs executive/avoidant; Baker gaming. Scaffolding that never fades isn't scaffolding.

items.stem: A newcomer learns cooking by watching and pitching in beside a more experienced cook, not by hearing a lecture about cooking. Rogoff's idea?

choices.text: Guided participation — join real activity with more experienced people.
Faultless communication — scripts remove all confusion by design.
Image Principle — film the cook's face next to the recipe.
Positive punishment — add disliked chores for mistakes.

items.explain: Rogoff guided participation. Related: Lave & Wenger LPP for community peripheries.

items.stem: A newbie does real but low-stakes tasks the group actually needs, then moves toward harder central work. Lave and Wenger?

choices.text: Legitimate peripheral participation — real edge work, then inward.
Assimilation — bend new tasks to an old solo schema.
Variable-ratio likes for forum posts.
Expertise reversal — worked examples hurt novices.

items.explain: LPP. Expertise reversal: worked examples help novices more; advantage shrinks with expertise.

items.stem: One idea is the gap between alone and with help. Another is temporary support inside that gap that should disappear. Split?

choices.text: Zone of proximal development is the gap; scaffolding is the temporary help in the gap.
Scaffolding is the gap; ZPD is any permanent tutor feature.
They are synonyms Joyner treats as identical.
ZPD is only a person; tools can never sit in that role.

items.explain: ZPD = zone; scaffolding = support (+ fade). MKO can be a tool. Never-fading help isn't scaffolding.

items.stem: Joyner's ESPN Top 10 vs Not Top 10: one student hunts the highlight reel; another only tries not to make the blooper reel. Goal orientations?

choices.text: Performance-approach vs performance-avoidance — same dunk scene, different aim.
Mastery vs belonging — both about understanding for its own sake.
Intrinsic vs germane load — both about working memory channels.
Classical vs operant — both about involuntary drool.

items.explain: Performance-approach = look competent; performance-avoidance = don't look dumb. Mastery = understand.

items.stem: Deci pays some students to solve puzzles; later free-play, the paid group plays less. Motivation lesson?

choices.text: External reward can undercut later intrinsic interest (overjustification); autonomy matters.
Any reward always raises long-run intrinsic motivation.
Puzzles prove learning styles: visual solvers need diagrams.
This is classical conditioning of puzzle fear.

items.explain: Deci 1971 / overjustification; SDT wants autonomy, competence, relatedness.

items.stem: Students hear that feeling out of place is normal and temporary. Grades and belonging can rise. Who/what?

choices.text: Walton and Cohen belonging intervention.
Engelmann faultless communication scripts.
Pashler learning-styles meshing.
Skinner programmed instruction frames.

items.explain: Belonging (Walton & Cohen). Learning-styles meshing failed (Pashler et al.).

items.stem: Remote proctoring systems struggled more with darker-skinned faces; students cannot easily leave the tool. Ethics framing?

choices.text: Bias in the tool becomes the learning experience; harm falls on people who cannot opt out.
Consent apps make school tools the same as consumer apps.
This proves visual learners need different proctors.
Only evaluation is affected; assessment never carries bias.

items.explain: Joyner ethics: prevent harm when users can't leave; bias becomes the experience (proctoring example).

items.stem: A poorly designed edtech tool helps students who are already ahead first; the gap grows. Reich's label?

choices.text: EdTech Matthew effect — advantages accrue to the already-resourced.
Expertise reversal — worked examples hurt experts only.
Hard fun — kids seek meaningful difficulty.
Fluency illusion — rereading feels like knowing.

items.explain: Reich EdTech Matthew effect. Other terms are real but different lessons.

items.stem: A designer wants to mesh 'visual vs auditory learners' with matching media. Course stance?

choices.text: Learning-styles meshing is a myth; real differences are prior knowledge, language, access, disability.
Meshing is required by ADA as the main accessibility strategy.
Visual learners always need the Image Principle face video.
Auditory learners should never get diagrams.

items.explain: Pashler et al. 2008 — meshing hypothesis failed. Accessibility ≠ learning-styles marketing.

items.stem: Heart-rate on one student for feedback vs using those readings to judge which workout plan works for the next cohort. Joyner's split?

choices.text: Assessment serves this learner's grade/feedback; evaluation judges the tool or curriculum.
Evaluation is always unethical; assessment is always fine.
They are dictionary synonyms Joyner forbids distinguishing.
Assessment means only multiple choice; evaluation means only essays.

items.explain: Course construct from Module 0: same measure, different why. Do not correct outsiders who swap the words.

items.stem: Essay help goes full worksheet → short reminder → gone. Support that never leaves would mean?

choices.text: It is not scaffolding — the tool keeps doing the work; fading was never designed in.
It is ideal ZPD because the zone should never move.
It is negative reinforcement of writing quality.
It is Capital-D DI because Project Follow Through used worksheets.

items.explain: Scaffolding requires planned removal. ZPD moves as competence grows.

items.stem: Scratch (2007, Lifelong Kindergarten / MIT Media Lab) shows up in the constructionism lineage. What is it for in Joyner's story?

choices.text: Block coding so different people make different personally meaningful projects — floor/ceiling plus Resnick's wide walls.
A Pavlov teaching machine with frames and immediate drool rewards.
Engelmann's choral-response reading script.
Mayer's rule that instructor faces always raise learning.

items.explain: Scratch = constructionist medium at scale. Not DI, not classical conditioning, not Image Principle.

items.stem: Papert criticizes the idea that improving learning mostly means improving how teachers explain and lecture. Name that foil?

choices.text: Instructionism — better transmission as the whole fix; counter is better materials to build with.
Constructivism — rebuild mental models.
Metacognition — monitor your own understanding.
Flow — challenge matched to skill.

items.explain: Instructionism is Papert's named foil. Constructionism answers with materials/making.

items.stem: A chess expert sees a board as a few meaningful patterns; a novice sees many separate pieces. Cognitivist account?

choices.text: Expertise packs elements into chunks so working memory holds more structure.
Experts have unlimited working memory slots by birth.
Only variable-ratio rewards create chess skill.
Chess skill is classical conditioning of piece fear.

items.explain: Miller/Cowan + chunking; expertise as richer chunks (Joyner cognitivism).
